title: Board of Regents of State Colleges v. Roth
lead: A first-year professor finishes his promised appointment but receives no renewal, reasons, or hearing; his hearing claim and his allegation of retaliation take different paths.

actors.name: David Roth
actors.role: First-year assistant professor at Wisconsin State University–Oshkosh.

actors.name: Board of Regents and university authorities
actors.role: Officials who declined renewal and defended the decision.

proceedings: The district court gave Roth partial summary judgment requiring reasons and a hearing, reserving the alleged retaliatory motive for trial.
The Seventh Circuit affirmed with one dissent.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded the procedural ruling; the speech claim remained unresolved.
limits: The case concerns nonrenewal after completion of a term, not midterm dismissal. Retaliation remained an allegation. Shared separate opinions appear after Perry in the report; Powell did not participate.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Roth receives an appointment for one academic year
sections.cue: What employment security did the appointment and university rules actually supply?
paragraphs: David Roth began his first teaching position as an assistant professor at Wisconsin State University–Oshkosh on September 1, 1968. The formal appointment notice operated as his contract, although no separate instrument existed. It secured employment through June 30, 1969, without promising renewal or requiring cause for a later nonrenewal.

Wisconsin law granted permanent employment after four continuous years, conditioned on efficiency and good behavior, and protected permanent teachers against discharge without cause and specified procedures. Roth had not acquired that status. Rules gave nontenured faculty some review of dismissal during an existing year but distinguished dismissal from nonretention for the next. They required nonretention notice by February 1 and expressly dispensed with reasons and review.

Before that deadline the president notified Roth that he would not return for 1969–1970. Roth completed the promised term. The university gave no reasons or hearing, but on this record made no charge of dishonesty, immorality, or similar misconduct harming his standing, and imposed no bar to other university jobs. Roth alleged retaliation for criticizing the administration; the officials denied it. Douglas later described controversy over suspended students, but the Supreme Court did not find that criticism caused nonrenewal.

sections.title: Roth wins a hearing order while the motive remains disputed
sections.cue: What precisely reached the Supreme Court?
paragraphs: Roth sued in federal district court on both a substantive free-speech theory and procedural due process. The court granted partial summary judgment requiring reasons and a hearing but reserved the true motive for trial. It balanced Roth’s substantial interest in reemployment against the university’s interest in summary action. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, one judge dissenting, and the university authorities obtained Supreme Court review.

Justice Stewart, writing for five Justices, confined the case to whether the present record established a constitutional right to reasons and a hearing. The university’s possible retaliation was not a resolved fact. The Court’s task was to identify a protected liberty or property interest before deciding what procedure would be due.

sections.title: Stewart looks first for liberty or property
sections.cue: Why did the importance of keeping the job not settle the procedural question?
paragraphs: The Court rejected the old idea that government could escape due process by calling public benefits privileges. Employment and benefits can be property, and liberty extends beyond freedom from physical restraint. But the threshold concerns the nature of the interest government has taken. Balancing its importance against administrative needs helps design process only after a protected deprivation is identified; need, desire, and unilateral expectation do not alone create entitlement.

The liberty analysis asked what accompanied this nonrenewal. Seriously damaging accusations, such as dishonesty or immorality, could require a chance to clear one’s name. Government-imposed barriers to a broader range of work could implicate occupational liberty. The record established neither. Loss of one position, even if it made Roth somewhat less appealing to another employer, did not itself establish governmental foreclosure of his career. The lower courts’ assumption of such foreclosure lacked evidentiary support. Actual blacklisting or damaging charges would present a different record.

A name-clearing hearing also would not automatically confer tenure. Refuting a charge leaves an employer potentially free to deny renewal for another permissible reason. Stewart thus separated the interest protected by a procedure from a substantive right to the job.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning; 408 U.S. 570–575 & nn.9–14

sections.title: The promised year differs from a promise of renewal
sections.cue: What independent source could have established a property interest?
paragraphs: Property arises from independent rules or understandings supporting a legitimate claim of entitlement. Statutory welfare eligibility, tenure rules, an unexpired contract term, or implied assurances of continued employment can supply it. A claimant need not win the underlying dispute first: Goldberg’s recipients possessed a statutory entitlement framework even though a hearing was needed to decide eligibility. The problem for Roth was the absence of a framework securing another year at all.

His appointment protected the stated year, which he completed. No statute, rule, policy, or established understanding in this record protected renewal. Roth argued that annual appointees generally returned, but the lower courts had not found that practice created a binding institutional common law. Frequent renewal and an enforceable entitlement were different matters. The Court expressly referred to Perry’s recognition that sufficiently established understandings could matter; it did not make formal written tenure indispensable.

Roth’s speech claim remained distinct. Lack of entitlement did not authorize retaliatory nonrenewal. The Court declined to infer a general hearing right simply from an unproved motive allegation and surrounding controversy. It also expressed no view about whether good university administration should voluntarily provide reasons and hearings. Constitutional minimums did not decide institutional best practice.

sections.title: The separate writings would give process a broader role
sections.cue: How did the other Justices approach academic freedom, fairness, and state law?
paragraphs: Justice Douglas would affirm. He stressed academic freedom, the potential for concealed retaliation, and harm to a teacher’s future career. Reasons and a response opportunity could expose pretext without forcing an employee to sue just to discover the explanation. He treated practical nonrenewal consequences like dismissal and accepted academic proceedings with continuing federal responsibility for constitutional questions. He recognized that speech protection and sincerity of reasons required factfinding; he did not purport to resolve a motive never tried.

Justice Marshall accepted the general framework but read liberty and property more broadly. Government, he argued, must make fair, nonarbitrary employment decisions, and a person seeking public employment was entitled to it absent a government reason for refusal. That interest required reasons and an opportunity to contest facts without a separately proved promise. Reasons should already exist for legitimate decisions, suitable summary procedures could handle volume, and regularity could expose mistakes and strengthen public confidence. This was his proposed theory, not the majority’s entitlement rule.

Chief Justice Burger’s concurrence, printed after Perry and applying to both cases, emphasized state-law express or implied contracts. He proposed abstention when uncertain state contract law controlled the antecedent entitlement question; the Court did not order that disposition here. Brennan, joined by Douglas, adopted Marshall’s procedural conclusion and would affirm Roth’s summary judgment while directing additional relief in Perry. Powell took no part.

sections.title: Roth loses this partial judgment without losing his unresolved speech claim
sections.cue: What did the reversal actually establish?
paragraphs: On June 29, 1972, the Supreme Court reversed the Seventh Circuit and remanded. Roth had not established protected liberty or property sufficient for summary judgment requiring reasons and a hearing. The Court neither found a constitutionally permissible motive nor awarded damages or reinstatement. His separate retaliation dispute remained for development.

Roth addresses whether an interest receives procedural protection; Mathews addresses design of process after such an interest is accepted. Even an established employment interest does not automatically require a full predecision trial. Roth and Perry likewise distinguish a forbidden motive from an entitlement to procedure and from ultimate success on nonrenewal. Describing this case as permission to reject any nontenured teacher for any reason would erase those distinctions.
